summary: POC scoping focused on workload characterization for AegisPay conversational and extraction workloads. Agreed to run benchmarks (QPS/concurrency sweeps) using sample logs, define success criteria (latency P95 < 250ms for hosted, cost target $0.002/token), and explore Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs. Next steps: exchange logs, Redwood to provide test harness and pricing, schedule results review.
transcript:
Meeting header:
[00:00] Jordan Lee (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. With me is Priya, our SE.
[00:08] Marta Ruiz (AegisPay - CTO): Hi Jordan, hi Priya. Marta here, Devon and Samir are on from infra, Leah is here too.
[00:14] Priya Raman (Redwood SE): Quick agenda: workload characterization, token distributions, propose benchmark sweep (QPS/concurrency), and define success criteria.
[00:22] Devon Park (Head of ML Platform): Cool, we've been getting a lot of requests for automated dispute handling and a few extraction pipelines. Main question is scale — currently average sustained RPS is around 12, peaks to about 120 during batch processing windows.
[00:34] Samir Patel (SRE): To add, concurrency when we hit the spikes is more like 80 to 120 simultaneous sessions, but many are short.
[00:40] Jordan Lee: Great, this call is mostly to map that into an inference sizing plan. Can you walk us through the input/output token characteristics?
[00:48] Devon Park: Sure. For our dispute assistant, average input length is 180 tokens, median 120, heavy tails up to 800 tokens for attachments + context. Output is usually shorter, 40 to 120 tokens for summary, but for some extraction flows we request 300-400 tokens.
[01:05] Priya Raman: That distribution matters a lot for batching and KV cache behavior. If you have many short responses, you get better throughput per GPU. Longer outputs push up latency and token cost.
[01:12] Leah Kim (PM): Our success criteria are a mix: P95 end-to-end latency under 250 ms for interactive flows, cost target roughly $0.002 per user message on average, and correctness metrics (F1 for extraction) staying within 2% of current baseline.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: Good explicit targets. For POC we'll validate latency and cost under a representative traffic mix. Typical POC plan we propose: 1) baseline profiling with 10 QPS, 2) ramp to 50 QPS, 3) 100 QPS peak tests with concurrency sweeps and different model variants.
[01:38] Marta Ruiz: That aligns with our expectations. What models are we testing? We want something close to our on-prem 70B variant but cheaper if possible.
[01:45] Priya Raman: For that profile we recommend testing two variants: an optimized 70B 4-bit quantized model (on Dedicated) and a 13B quantized model (hosted) as a fallback. We'll also look at sequence-length performance and per-token throughput numbers.
[01:56] Devon Park: Can Redwood emulate our 70B perf on hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[02:02] Jordan Lee: We can run 70B on our Dedicated cluster with guaranteed capacity — that gives you predictable latency. Hosted can serve smaller quantized models; we can also test a relaxed version of 70B depending on availability.
[02:12] Samir Patel: From security side we need VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, and SOC2 SOC-two artifacts — encryption at rest and audit logs.
[02:20] Priya Raman: Noted. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs; for Hosted we can arrange a private tenancy or Dedicated to meet those requirements. We'll attach our SOC 2 and ISO docs to the notes.
[02:30] Leah Kim: Regarding traffic modeling — we can share logs, but we need to anonymize PII. What format do you need?
[02:36] Priya Raman: A simple CSV with columns: timestamp, input_token_count, output_token_count, response_time_ms (optional), and a request type tag. That lets us generate a synthetic replay with the same token distribution and time-of-day arrival pattern.
[02:47] Devon Park: Ok we'll extract two weeks of logs and scrub PII. Expect that by Monday.
[02:52] Jordan Lee: For benchmarking metrics, we'll measure: P50/P95 latency, tail latency P99, throughput (QPS), tokens/sec per GPU, and cost per request. We'll also run quality checks — run the same prompts through your eval set to verify output fidelity.
[03:06] Marta Ruiz: On the cost side, we want to compare unit economics: hosted per-token vs Dedicated amortized GPU cost including utilization assumptions.
[03:14] Priya Raman: We'll provide cost models in the spreadsheet. For Dedicated sizing we'll show GPU counts based on concurrency and token throughput, and for Hosted we'll show estimated spend at target QPS.
[03:22] Jordan Lee: A realistic POC test plan — Priya, can you outline the exact runs you'd perform?
[03:27] Priya Raman: Sure. Proposed runs:
- Warmup pass at low QPS (10) for 10 minutes to prime caches.
- Steady-state tests at 10/25/50 QPS for 15 minutes each.
- Concurrency sweep: hold QPS and increase concurrent sessions to match your observed 80-120 range.
- Peak burst tests: simulate your batch window pattern (120 RPS for 10 minutes).
- Latency SLO verification: measure P95 and P99 across runs.
- Quality regression: run 500 sample prompts through both models and compute extraction F1.
[03:55] Samir Patel: For the synthetic replay will you respect inter-arrival times to reproduce concurrency?
[03:59] Priya Raman: Yes, we'll replay timestamps and also do a poisson-modeled variant to stress concurrency.
[04:05] Leah Kim: One point — we have a long-tail of requests with 800+ tokens, do you recommend conditioning or truncation?
[04:11] Priya Raman: We recommend a mixed strategy: prefix summarization or chunking for retrieval-heavy contexts, and for the POC we should include some of the long-tail to show performance impact.
[04:20] Devon Park: How long does a POC typically run and cost estimate?
[04:23] Jordan Lee: Typical POC is 2-3 weeks: first week for data transfer and setup, second week for benchmark runs and analysis. Cost depends on duration of Dedicated capacity; rough estimate for a 2-week Dedicated test with a 70B profile could be in the low tens of thousands, but we'll provide a precise estimate once we size GPUs. Hosted tests for 13B are cheaper and can be done with usage billing.
[04:40] Marta Ruiz: Can you give an example of the sizing math? If we want to support 100 QPS with P95 < 250ms, what's the starting point?
[04:49] Priya Raman: Example: if a single GPU can handle 20 tokens/ms and your average end-to-end token generation per request is 300 tokens, that's 15,000 tokens per request; sorry that's incorrect, let me rephrase—if it's 300 tokens output and 180 input that's 480 tokens total. If gpu throughput is 10k tokens/sec, that translates to ~20 req/sec per GPU. So for 100 QPS you'd need ~5 GPUs with headroom for bursts. Quantization and batching can change those numbers by 1.5-2x.
[05:17] Devon Park: That math helps. We will share token distribution so you can run accurate per-GPU throughput sims.
[05:22] Jordan Lee: On success criteria — Leah if you can draft a short doc with prioritized KPIs that will serve as our acceptance test. You mentioned latency, cost, and accuracy.
[05:30] Leah Kim: Yes I'll draft and share tomorrow.
[05:33] Samir Patel: Are there any network requirements for VPC peering? We use AWS and would prefer peering over open internet for PII.
[05:39] Priya Raman: We support AWS VPC peering and private link. We'll put the network playbook into the notes. For KMS, we support external CMKs via our Private/ Dedicated offering.
[05:49] Marta Ruiz: Regarding the benchmark harness, will Redwood run it or do we run it from our end?
[05:54] Priya Raman: Redwood can run the harness from our side to provide an apples-to-apples comparison, but it's best if your SRE can run it from your network to validate latency/bandwidth impacts. We can do both.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: Anything else on tradeoffs? We should call out that hosted is faster to start but Dedicated gives you more predictable tail latency and isolation.
[06:13] Devon Park: And Dedicated means more work upfront but predictable cost if utilization is high.
[06:17] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. Let's confirm dates: Devon will send logs by Monday (2026-08-17), Priya and Jordan will send benchmark plan by Tuesday (2026-08-18), Leah will share success criteria by Wednesday (2026-08-19), and we'll reconvene on 2026-08-25 for results.
[06:31] Jordan Lee: Perfect. I'll attach SOC2 and a sample benchmark spreadsheet to the meeting notes.
[06:37] Priya Raman: I'll prepare the load scripts (k6/locust) and a dockerized runner for replay. Also will include an example synthetic distribution generator.
[06:46] Leah Kim: Quick question — are you able to demonstrate quantized 70B perf or is that internal testing?
[06:50] Priya Raman: We have internal perf numbers and can run it in Dedicated for the POC; we'll show real numbers in the benchmark. Hosted availability depends on capacity but we can use a 13B hosted baseline.
[06:59] Marta Ruiz: Thanks all, this is helpful.
[07:02] Jordan Lee: Recap of next steps: logs from AegisPay, benchmark plan and scripts from Redwood, success criteria doc from Leah, and schedule 8/25 for result review. We'll follow up with calendar invites.
[07:15] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional word swaps (e.g., "ten QPS" vs "10 QPS"), speaker labels simplified, some overlapping talk snippets. References: benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in notes), SOC2 package (link), sample load scripts (link).
